1
清起東陲，太宗設文館，命達海等繙譯經史。 復改國史、祕書、弘文三院，編纂國史，收藏書籍，文教始興。 世祖入定中原，命馮銓等議修明史，復詔求遺書。 聖祖繼統，詔舉博學鴻儒，修經史，纂圖書，稽古右文，潤色鴻業，海內彬彬向風焉。 高宗繼試鴻詞，博採遺籍，特命輯修四庫全書，以皇子永瑢、大學士于敏中等為總裁，紀昀、陸錫熊等為總纂，與其事者三百餘人，皆極一時之選，歷二十年始告成。 全書三萬六千冊，繕寫七部，分藏大內文淵閣，圓明園文源閣，盛京文溯閣，熱河文津閣，揚州文匯閣，鎮江文宗閣，杭州文瀾閣。 命紀昀等撰全書總目，著錄三千四百五十八種，存目六千七百八十八種，都一萬二百四十六種。 覆命于敏中、王際華擷其精華，別為四庫薈要，凡一萬二千冊，分繕二部，藏之大內摛藻堂及御園味腴書屋。 又別輯永樂大典三百八十五種，交武英殿以聚珍版印行。 時大典儲翰林院者尚存二萬四百七十三卷，合九千八百八十一冊。 其宋、元精槧，多儲內府，天祿琳琅，備詳宮史。 經籍既盛，學術斯昌，文治之隆，漢、唐以來所未逮也。 各省先後進書，約及萬種，阮元既補四庫未收書四百五十四種，復刊經解一千四百十二卷，王先謙又刊續經解一千三百十五卷，而各省督撫，廣修方誌，郡邑典章，粲然大備。 其後曾國籓倡設金陵、蘇州、揚州、杭州、武昌官書局，張之洞設廣雅書局，延聘儒雅，校刊群籍，私家亦輯刻日多，叢書之富，曩代莫京。 及至晚近，歐風東漸，競譯西書，道藝並重。 而敦煌寫經，殷墟龜甲，奇書祕寶，考古所資，其有裨於學術者尤多，實集古今未有之盛焉。 藝文舊例，胥列古籍，茲仿明史為志，凡所著錄，斷自清代。 唯清人輯古佚書甚夥，不可略之，則附載各類之後。
When the Qing rose from the northeastern marches, Emperor Taizong founded a Literary Institute and charged Dahai and others with translating the classics and historical works. The office was later reorganized as three bureaus—National History, Secretariat, and Hongwen—charged with compiling dynastic history and curating books, and formal literary culture took root. After the Shunzhi Emperor established rule over China proper, he commissioned Feng Quan and others to plan a revision of the History of Ming and again ordered a search for lost books. When the Kangxi Emperor came to the throne, he summoned eminent scholars, undertook revision of the classics and histories, and organized imperial bibliographic projects; by honoring antiquity and elevating learning he adorned the dynasty's achievement, and scholars across the empire turned toward culture in growing numbers. The Qianlong Emperor continued the special literary examinations, gathered surviving texts on a vast scale, and ordered the compilation of the Siku Quanshu (Complete Library in Four Treasuries), with Prince Yong Rong and Grand Secretary Yu Minzhong as chief directors and Ji Yun and Lu Xixiong as chief compilers; over three hundred participants, all leading scholars of the day, worked for twenty years before the project was finished. The complete collection ran to thirty-six thousand volumes, transcribed in seven copies and housed in the Wenyuan, Wenyuan (Yuanmingyuan), Wenshu, Wenjin, Wenhui, Wenzong, and Wenlan pavilions at the capital, Mukden, Rehe, Yangzhou, Zhenjiang, and Hangzhou respectively. Ji Yun and others were commissioned to compile the general catalogue, which listed 3,458 works in full entries, 6,788 in a supplementary register, for a total of 10,246 titles. Yu Minzhong and Wang Jihua were then directed to distill the finest portions into the Siku Huiyao (Essentials of the Four Treasuries), twelve thousand volumes in two copies, kept in the Chizao Hall and the Weiyu Library. Three hundred eighty-five works were also excerpted from the Yongle Dadian and sent to the Wuying Hall for publication in the imperial Movable-Type Treasury series. At that time the Hanlin Academy copy of the encyclopedia still comprised 20,473 juan in 9,881 fascicles. Choice Song and Yuan imprints were largely held in the inner palace; the Tianlu Linlang catalogue preserves a detailed record of the court collection. With the classics and books in such abundance, scholarship flourished; the brilliance of literary rule surpassed anything known since Han and Tang times. Provinces in turn presented books totaling roughly ten thousand titles; Ruan Yuan added 454 works omitted from the Siku collection and reprinted 1,412 juan of classical commentaries, and Wang Xianqian published a further 1,315 juan of supplementary commentaries, while governors and lieutenant-governors throughout the empire revised local gazetteers until county and prefectural records were comprehensively in order. Later Zeng Guofan sponsored official publishing bureaus at Nanjing, Suzhou, Yangzhou, Hangzhou, and Wuchang; Zhang Zhidong founded the Guangya Press and engaged eminent scholars to collate and print books, while private compilations and editions multiplied; never had collected series been so abundant. In later times Western learning reached China from the east, Western books were translated in great number, and moral philosophy and practical science were pursued with equal seriousness. Dunhuang manuscript scrolls, Yin-dynasty oracle bones from Anyang, and other rare treasures furnished new materials for archaeology and greatly advanced scholarship, bringing together a concentration of learning unparalleled in history. Earlier bibliographic treatises listed ancient works in general; following the model of the History of Ming, this treatise records only works of the Qing dynasty. Because Qing scholars compiled so many collections of lost ancient texts, however, these are appended after each category rather than omitted.

經部十類：一曰易類，二曰書類，三曰詩類，四曰禮類，五曰樂類，六曰春秋類，七曰孝經類，八曰四書類，九曰經總義類，十曰小學類。
The Classics section comprises ten categories: (1) Changes, (2) Documents, (3) Odes, (4) Rites, (5) Music, (6) Spring and Autumn, (7) Classic of Filial Piety, (8) Four Books, (9) general commentaries on the classics, and (10) philology.

清代肇基東陲，造創伊始，文教未宏。 太宗首命大學士希福等譯遼、金、元三史，逮世祖譯史告成，二年又有議修明史之詔。 惟其時區宇未寧，日不暇給，是以石渠之建，猶未遑焉。 聖祖繼統，詔舉博學鴻儒，繼修明史，復纂諸經解、圖書集成等書，以網羅遺逸，拔擢英才，宏獎斯文，潤色鴻業，馴致太平之治，而海內彬彬靡然向風矣。 世宗嗣位，再舉鴻詞，未行而崩。
When the Qing dynasty rose in the northeast, literary culture was still in its infancy. Emperor Taizong first charged Grand Secretary Hifu and others with translating the Liao, Jin, and Yuan histories; after the Shunzhi Emperor completed the translation project, an edict was issued in the second year to plan revision of the History of Ming. The realm was still unsettled and the court had scarcely a moment to spare, so the Shiqu library project had not yet been attempted. When the Kangxi Emperor came to the throne, he summoned eminent scholars, continued work on the History of Ming, and commissioned compilations including classical commentaries and the Complete Collection of Books to recover lost texts, promote talent, and encourage learning; by adorning the dynasty achievement he brought about an age of peace, and scholars across the empire turned toward culture in growing numbers. When the Yongzheng Emperor succeeded to the throne, he planned another special literary examination, but died before it could be held.
58
高宗初元，繼試鴻博，採訪遺書。 乾隆三十七年諭曰：「朕稽古右文，聿資治理，幾餘典學，日有孜孜。 因思策府縹緗，載籍極博，其鉅者羽翼經訓，垂範方來，固足稱千秋法鑒，即在識小之徒，專門撰述，細及名物象數，兼綜條貫，各自成家，亦莫不有所發明，可為遊藝養心之助。 然或逸在名山，未登柱史，正宜及時採集，匯送京師，以彰千古同文之盛。 其令直省督撫、學政加意購訪，量為給價，家藏鈔本，錄副呈送。 庶幾藏在石渠，用儲乙覽，四庫、七略益昭美備，稱朕意焉。」 於是安徽學政朱筠條奏明永樂大典內多古書，請開局纂輯，繕寫各自為書。 時永樂大典儲翰林院，已有殘缺，原書為卷二萬二千九百三十七，缺二千四百四卷，存二萬四百七十三卷，為冊九千八百八十一。 高宗下筠議，大學士于敏中力贊其說。 明年，詔設四庫全書館，以皇子永瑢、大學士于敏中等為總裁，侍郎紀昀、大理寺卿陸錫熊等為總纂，其纂修等官則有戴震、邵晉涵、庄存與、任大椿、王念孫、姚鼐、翁方綱、朱筠等，與事者三百餘人，皆博選一時之俊。 歷二十年，始繕寫告成。 先後編輯之書三百八十五種，以聚珍版印行百餘種。 三十九年，催繳直省藏書，四方競進秘籍甚眾，江、浙督撫采進者達四五千種，浙江鮑士恭、范懋柱、汪啟淑，江蘇馬裕家藏之籍，呈進者各六七百種，周厚育、蔣曾瑩、吳玉墀、孫仰曾、汪汝瑮等亦各進書百種以上。 至是天府之藏，卓越前代，特命紀昀等撰四庫全書總目，著錄三千四百五十八種，存目著錄六千七百八十八種，都一萬二百四十六種。 復以總目提要卷帙浩繁，學子繙閱匪易，又命紀昀就總目之書別纂四庫簡明目錄，其存目之書不預焉。
At the beginning of the Qianlong reign, the emperor resumed the special literary examinations and searched out lost books. In the thirty-seventh year of Qianlong (1772) he issued an instruction: "By examining antiquity and honoring letters I support good governance; in my spare moments I study the classics with unflagging diligence. He reflected that the imperial library held vast stores of learning: the greatest works uphold the classics and set standards for ages to come, worthy to serve as models for a thousand years; even specialized treatises on names, objects, and numbers, each forming its own school of thought, contain discoveries that enrich the mind and furnish cultured recreation. Yet some works still lie hidden in remote places and have never entered the imperial archives; they should be collected promptly and sent to the capital to manifest the glory of a unified literary culture across the ages. He ordered governors-general, governors, and provincial education commissioners throughout the empire to search diligently for such works, pay fair prices, and have owners of manuscript copies submit transcribed duplicates. Thus they might be housed in the imperial library for the emperor review, making the Four Treasuries and Seven Summaries ever more splendidly complete, as I desire." Thereupon Zhu Yun, education commissioner of Anhui, memorialized that the Yongle Encyclopedia preserved many ancient works and requested that a compilation bureau be established to transcribe them as separate books. At that time the Yongle Encyclopedia held in the Hanlin Academy was already incomplete: the original comprised 22,937 juan, of which 2,404 were missing and 20,473 remained, bound in 9,881 fascicles. The Qianlong Emperor referred the proposal to Zhu Yun for discussion, and Grand Secretary Yu Minzhong strongly endorsed it. The following year an edict established the Siku Quanshu Bureau, with Prince Yong Rong and Grand Secretary Yu Minzhong as chief directors, Ji Yun and Lu Xixiong as chief compilers, and among the editors Dai Zhen, Shao Jinhan, Zhuang Cunyu, Ren Dachun, Wang Niansun, Yao Nai, Weng Fanggang, Zhu Yun, and others; over three hundred participants, all leading scholars of the day, were selected. After twenty years the transcription was completed. Three hundred eighty-five works were compiled in all, and more than one hundred were printed in the Movable-Type Treasury edition. In the thirty-ninth year (1774), the court urged provinces to submit holdings; rare books poured in from every direction. The Jiangsu and Zhejiang governors forwarded as many as four or five thousand titles; Bao Shigong, Fan Maozhu, and Wang Qishu of Zhejiang and Ma Yu of Jiangsu each presented six or seven hundred works from family collections; Zhou Houyu, Jiang Zengying, Wu Yuchi, Sun Yangzeng, Wang Rujiong, and others each submitted more than one hundred titles. By then the imperial collection surpassed all previous dynasties; Ji Yun and others were commissioned to compile the General Catalogue of the Siku Quanshu, listing 3,458 works in full entries and 6,788 in a supplementary register, for a total of 10,246 titles. Because the general catalogue and summaries were too voluminous for easy consultation, Ji Yun was directed to compile a separate Brief Catalogue of the Four Treasuries from the fully catalogued works; supplementary-list titles were excluded.
59
先是高宗命擷四庫精華，都四百六十四部，繕為薈要，藏諸摛藻堂，以備御覽。
Earlier the Qianlong Emperor had ordered the finest portions of the Four Treasuries distilled into 464 works, copied as the Essentials and kept in the Chizao Hall for imperial review.
60
當是時，四庫寫書至十六萬八千冊，詔鈔四分，分庋京師文淵、京西圓明園文源、奉天文溯、熱河文津四閣，復簡選精要，命武英殿刊版頒行。 四十七年，詔再寫三分，分貯揚州大觀堂之文匯閣、鎮江金山寺之文宗閣、杭州聖因寺玉蘭堂之文瀾閣，令好古之士欲讀中秘書者，任其入覽。 用是海內從風，人文炳蔚，學術昌盛，方駕漢、唐。 後文源載籍燼於英法聯軍，文匯、文宗毀於洪楊之亂，文瀾亦有散佚。 獨文淵、文溯、文津三閣之書，巍然具存，書皆鈔本，其宋、元精刊，多儲大內天祿琳琅等處，載諸宮史； 而外省督撫，禮聘儒雅，廣修方誌，郡邑典章，粲然大備。 阮元補四庫未收書四百五十四種，復刊學海堂經解一千四百十二卷，王先謙續刊一千三百十五卷，甄采精博，一代經學人文萃焉。 曾國籓督兩江，倡設金陵、蘇州、揚州、浙江、武昌官書局，張之洞督粵，設廣雅書局，皆慎選通儒，審校群籍，廣為剞劂，以惠士林，而私家校勘，精鏤亦夥，叢書之富，曩代莫京。
At that time the Siku transcription reached 168,000 fascicles; an edict ordered four copies deposited in the Wenyuan, Wenyuan (Yuanmingyuan), Wenshu, and Wenjin pavilions; selected essentials were sent to the Wuying Hall for block printing and distribution. In the forty-seventh year (1782) an edict ordered three additional copies for the Wenhui, Wenzong, and Wenlan pavilions at Yangzhou, Zhenjiang, and Hangzhou, permitting scholars who wished to consult palace holdings to read them on site. Thereupon scholars across the empire followed suit; literary culture flourished and scholarship prospered, rivaling Han and Tang times. Later the Wenyuan collection was destroyed by the Anglo-French allied forces; the Wenhui and Wenzong libraries were lost in the Taiping Rebellion; the Wenlan collection also suffered dispersal. Only the Wenyuan, Wenshu, and Wenjin collections survived intact, all in manuscript; fine Song and Yuan editions were largely held in the inner palace collections such as Tianlu Linlang, as recorded in palace histories; while provincial governors engaged eminent scholars, extensively revised local gazetteers, and brought county and prefectural records comprehensively up to date. Ruan Yuan added 454 works omitted from the Siku collection and reprinted 1,412 juan of classical commentaries at the Xuehai Hall; Wang Xianqian published a further 1,315 juan; their selections were precise and comprehensive, gathering the scholarship of an age. Zeng Guofan, as governor-general of Liangjiang, sponsored official publishing bureaus at Nanjing, Suzhou, Yangzhou, Zhejiang, and Wuchang; Zhang Zhidong, as governor-general of Guangdong, founded the Guangya Press; all engaged eminent scholars to collate and print books widely for the benefit of scholars, while private editions also multiplied; never had collected series been so abundant.
61
清之末葉，歐風東漸，科學日昌。 同治初，設江南製造局，始譯西籍。 光緒末，復設譯書局，流風所被，譯書競出，憂世俊英，群研時務。 是時敦煌寫經，殷墟龜甲，異書秘寶，胥見塏壤，實足獻納藝林，宏裨學術，其間碩學名儒，各標宗派，故鴻篇鉅制，不可殫紀。
In the late Qing period, Western learning spread eastward and modern science advanced daily. In the early Tongzhi era the Jiangnan Arsenal was established and Western books began to appear in Chinese translation. Late in the Guangxu era a translation bureau was established; translations proliferated, and concerned scholars applied themselves collectively to contemporary affairs. Dunhuang manuscripts, Yin-dynasty oracle bones from Anyang, and other rare treasures emerged from the ground, richly furnishing the world of learning; eminent scholars each founded their own schools, and great works beyond numbering were produced.
62
藝文舊例，胥列古籍，清代總目，既已博載，茲志著錄，取則明史，斷自清代。 四部分類，多從總目，審例訂譌，間有異撰。 清儒箸述，總目所載，捊采靡遺，存目稍蕪，斠錄從慎。 乾隆以前，漏者補之，嘉慶以後，缺者續之，苟有纖疑，則從蓋闕。 前朝群書，例既弗錄，清代輯佚，異乎斯旨，裒纂功深，無殊撰述，故附載焉。
Earlier bibliographic treatises listed ancient works in general; the Qing general catalogue already records abundantly; this treatise follows the History of Ming and limits entries to the Qing dynasty. The fourfold classification largely follows the general catalogue, with categories reviewed and errors corrected, though occasional divergences appear. Qing scholars works listed in the general catalogue were gathered exhaustively; the supplementary register is somewhat diffuse, and entries were collated with caution. Omissions before the Qianlong era were supplied; gaps after the Jiaqing era were filled in; where the slightest doubt remained, entries were deliberately omitted. Works of earlier dynasties are by rule not recorded; Qing recovery of lost texts follows a different principle, yet the labor of compilation equals original authorship; therefore such works are appended.
